title: Flat and solid: 2D and 3D shapes, and a flat creature's world

summary.text: Cut a round potato straight across, and the cut side is a flat circle. A solid shape, like a potato or a box, has three directions: length, width and height. A flat shape, like a circle drawn on paper, has only two: length and width. A creature who lived in a flat world could move forward, back, left and right, but never up. She would meet a solid potato one flat slice at a time.
summary.art: A girl at a kitchen counter tracing round a slice of potato on paper, with a row of traced circles of different sizes beside her.

intro.hook: Look at a round potato. If a grown-up cuts it straight across, what shape will the cut side be? Will every slice be the same size?
intro.text: A potato is solid. You can hold it, turn it and look at it from all sides. But the cut side of a slice is flat, like a drawing. In this unit you hunt for flat and solid things at home. You slice vegetables and trace the flat shapes hidden inside them. You look along a table with your eye flat to it, the way a flat creature would see. You open a box out flat, and fold it back into a solid.
intro.art: A whole potato, a cucumber and a carrot on a chopping board, with question marks over each one.

outcomes: By the end I can tell a flat (2D) shape from a solid (3D) shape, and say that a solid has length, width and height.
By the end I can name a sphere, a cube, a cuboid, a cylinder and a cone, and find the flat faces on a solid.
By the end I can show that cutting a solid gives a flat shape, and that the shape depends on where I cut.
By the end I can open a box out into a flat net, and fold a net back into a box.
By the end I can say what a flat creature could and could not do, and what she would see.
By the end I can say that even paper is a very thin solid, and that nobody knows if there are more than three directions.

terms.meaning: A flat shape has length and width, but no height at all. 2D means two dimensions. Circles, squares, triangles and rectangles are flat shapes.
terms.example: A circle drawn on paper, or the lines of a kolam on the floor.
terms.art: A circle, a square, a triangle and a rectangle drawn in chalk on a floor.

terms.meaning: A solid shape has length, width and height. 3D means three dimensions. A solid takes up space, and you can hold it.
terms.example: A ball, a steel tumbler, a matchbox and a ladoo are all solid shapes.
terms.art: A ball, a steel tumbler, a matchbox and a ladoo standing in a row on a table.

terms.meaning: A dimension is one direction you can measure. Length is how long a thing is. Width is how wide it is, from side to side. Height is how tall it is, from bottom to top.
terms.example: A matchbox has a length, a width and a height. You can measure each with a ruler.
terms.art: A matchbox with three coloured arrows along it: one for length, one for width, one for height.

terms.meaning: A face is one flat side of a solid shape.
terms.example: A dice has 6 faces. Each face is a square with dots on it.
terms.art: A dice with one square face shaded.

terms.meaning: An edge is the line where two faces of a solid meet.
terms.example: Run your finger along the sharp edge of a closed book.
terms.art: A finger running along the edge of a closed book.

terms.meaning: A slice is a thin piece cut from a solid. The cut side of a slice is a flat shape.
terms.example: A slice cut straight across a cucumber shows a flat circle.
terms.art: A cucumber with one round slice cut off, lying beside it.

terms.meaning: A net is a flat shape that can be folded up to make a solid.
terms.example: Open a toothpaste box out flat, and you get its net.
terms.art: A toothpaste box opened out flat into a long cross shape, next to a closed box.

terms.meaning: These are names for solid shapes. A sphere is round like a ball. A cube has 6 square faces. A cuboid is box-shaped. A cylinder is like a tube with round ends. A cone has a round base and a point.
terms.example: A ladoo is a sphere, a dice is a cube, a matchbox is a cuboid, a steel tumbler is nearly a cylinder, and a birthday cap is a cone.
terms.art: A ladoo, a dice, a matchbox, a steel tumbler and a birthday cap, each with its shape name under it.

explanations.context: This card explains flat and solid, after your hunt for flat and solid things at home.
explanations.definition: A flat (2D) shape has two dimensions: length and width. A solid (3D) shape has three dimensions: length, width and height.
explanations.description: In the hunt, you found things that look flat, like paper or a chapati, and things that are clearly solid, like a ball. A circle drawn on paper goes along the paper and across it, but not up. A steel tumbler goes up too, so it is a solid. You can hold a solid in your hand, but you can only draw a flat shape.
examples: A square drawn on a slate is a flat shape
A dice is a solid shape
A kolam on the floor is made of flat shapes
explanations.art: A square drawn on a slate next to a dice, with arrows showing two directions on the square and three on the dice.

explanations.context: This card explains the flat sides of solid shapes, after you opened out a box.
explanations.definition: A face is a flat side of a solid. An edge is where two faces meet.
explanations.description: Many solids have flat faces. A dice has 6 square faces, and a matchbox has 6 rectangle faces. A steel tumbler has one flat round face at the bottom, and a curved side. A ball has no flat face and no edge, so it rolls every way.
examples: A ball: no flat faces at all
explanations.art: A dice, a matchbox, a tumbler and a ball, with their flat faces shaded.

explanations.concept: Inside every solid are flat slices
explanations.context: This card explains what you found in the slice and trace test.
explanations.definition: When you cut straight through a solid, the cut side is a flat shape. Which flat shape you get depends on the solid, and on where and how you cut.
explanations.description: In the slice and trace test, the cucumber gave circles of nearly the same size. The carrot gave circles that got smaller towards the tip. The round potato gave small circles near the ends and the biggest in the middle. A corner cut off the potato cube gave a triangle. Stacked back up, the potato slices made the potato again.
examples: The middle slice of a round potato: the biggest circle
A corner cut off a cube: a triangle
explanations.art: A round potato cut into five slices, spread out in a row from small to big to small, with their traced circles below.

explanations.context: This card is about a made-up creature who lives in a flat world, like a drawing on paper. Thinking about her helps us see what our third direction does.
explanations.description: Imagine Pulli, a flat girl who lives on a sheet of paper. She can move forward, back, left and right, but there is no up for her. A pencil circle round her is a wall, because stepping over means going up. A ball passing down through her world would look like a dot, then a growing circle, then a shrinking one. Nobody has met a real flat creature. Scientists and writers use her to think with.
examples: A circle round Pulli locks her in
A coin on her paper looks like a line
A ball passing through looks like a circle that grows and shrinks
explanations.art: A small flat girl drawn on paper, inside a pencil circle, looking at a coin edge-on as a line.

explanations.context: This card is about a question people still argue about: can a real thing be truly flat?
explanations.description: A sheet of paper looks flat, but it has a tiny height. Stack 100 sheets and the pile is about 1 centimetre tall. A chapati and a dosa are thin solids too. Graphene is a sheet of carbon one atom thick, one of the thinnest materials made. Even one atom has some height, so people argue about whether anything real is truly 2D.
examples: A sheet of paper: a very thin solid
A pile of 100 sheets: about 1 centimetre tall
Graphene: a sheet one atom thick

perspectives.explanation: A truly flat shape, with no height at all, is an idea in our minds. We can draw it and think about it, but every real thing has some height.
Graphene is so thin that it behaves like a flat world. Tiny particles in it can move only along it and across it, not up. So they call it a 2D material.

explanations.art: A pile of 100 sheets of paper next to a ruler showing 1 centimetre, and one single sheet seen from the side as a thin line.

agreed.text: A flat shape has length and width. A solid shape has length, width and height.
agreed.evidence: In the hunt, every solid you held could be measured three ways with a ruler: long, wide and tall.

agreed.text: Cutting straight through a solid gives a flat shape, and the shape depends on where you cut.
agreed.evidence: In the slice and trace test, the round potato gave circles of different sizes, and a corner of the potato cube gave a triangle.

agreed.text: Many solids can be opened out into a flat net and folded back up.
agreed.evidence: In Open a Box, the box opened out flat, and folded back into the same box.

agreed.text: Every real thing has some height, even a sheet of paper.
agreed.evidence: 100 sheets of paper stacked up make a pile about 1 centimetre tall.

challenging.claim: The Earth is flat, like a huge plate.
challenging.who: Many people long ago, in many countries.
challenging.for: The ground around us looks flat, and the sea looks flat to the edge of the sky.
challenging.against: In an eclipse of the Moon, the Earth's shadow on the Moon is always round. Only a ball makes a round shadow from every side. Ships sailing away disappear from the bottom up. Today, photos from space show the round Earth.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea about the shape of the Earth.

challenging.claim: A thin thing like a sheet of paper or a dosa is a flat (2D) shape.
challenging.for: Paper and dosas are so thin that they look flat, and we draw flat shapes on paper.
challenging.against: Stack 100 sheets of paper, and the pile is about 1 centimetre tall. So each sheet has a tiny height, and is really a very thin solid.
challenging.context: This card is about a mistake many of us make at first.

challenging.claim: There may be more than three directions in space, too small or too hidden for us to notice.
challenging.who: Some physicists today. They work on ideas such as string theory.
challenging.for: Their sums about the tiniest parts of the world work better if there are extra directions.
challenging.against: Nobody has ever found an extra direction in any experiment. Many physicists think there are just three.
challenging.context: This card is about a big question scientists still argue about.

big_questions.q: Pulli the flat girl can never go up. Could she even imagine what up is?
big_questions.hint: Think how hard it is for you to imagine a direction that is not forward, sideways or up.

big_questions.q: Your potato slices stacked back into a potato. Is a solid just flat slices piled up?
big_questions.hint: Think of the stacked potato slices. Could you ever cut a slice so thin that it had no height?

big_questions.q: If there were a fourth direction, how might we find out?
big_questions.hint: How could Pulli find out about up? What would she see if a ball passed through her world?

big_questions.q: An ant walks on the floor and up the wall. Does an ant live in a flat world or a solid one?
big_questions.hint: Watch an ant. Does she ever go up off the surface she walks on?

big_questions.q: A leaf is thin and wide. Why might a plant spread their leaves so flat?
big_questions.hint: Think of what a leaf catches from the sky.

story.title: Kayal and Pulli, the Girl in the Kolam
story.note: Kayal, Sidhu and their Amma are made up. Pulli means dot in Tamil. A pulli kolam is a kolam drawn round rows of dots.
text: Every morning, Amma drew a kolam on the floor outside the door of their flat in Chennai. First she made rows of white dots with rice flour. Then she looped lines around the dots, without lifting her hand.
Kayal, who was in Class 2, sat on the step and watched. Her little brother Sidhu crouched next to her, with his chin on his knees.
"Who lives in the kolam?" Sidhu asked.
"Nobody," said Amma, smiling. "It's a drawing."
Kayal looked at one white dot. "Let's pretend someone does," she said. "A tiny flat girl called Pulli."
"Flat like a dosa?" asked Sidhu.

"Flatter," said Kayal. "You can lift a dosa off the tava. It has a top and a bottom. Pulli has no top and no bottom. She is like a drawing. She can go forward and back. She can go left and right. But she can never go up."
Sidhu frowned. "Never? Not even if she jumps?"
"There is no up in her world," said Kayal. "Up is a direction she has never seen."
That afternoon, Kayal took a sheet of paper and drew Pulli. She was a small round girl with a dot for an eye. Around her, Kayal drew a square house with a gap in one side for the door.
"Now watch," said Kayal. She drew a pencil line across the gap. "Pulli is locked in."
"Let her out!" said Sidhu. "She can just step over the line."

"Stepping over means going up, and then down again," said Kayal. "Pulli has no up. For her, a pencil line is a wall as high as the sky." She rubbed out the line with an eraser, and the door was open again.
Then Kayal put a one-rupee coin on the paper, next to Pulli's house. "What does Pulli see when she looks at the coin?"
Sidhu put his chin on the edge of the table, so that his eye was level with the paper. The round coin looked like a thin line.
"Just a line," he said. "She can't tell that the coin is round."

"She can, if she walks all the way round it," said Kayal. "A round coin looks the same width from every side. A square card looks wider when you look at it from a corner." She put a square of card beside the coin, and turned it. Sidhu watched the line get a little longer, then shorter again.

In the evening, Amma was cutting a lemon for rasam. Kayal and Sidhu watched her cut it across, slice by slice. Each slice was a circle. The slices near the ends were small. The slice in the middle was the biggest.
"Sidhu," said Kayal, "imagine the lemon pushed slowly down through Pulli's paper, like a needle through cloth. What would Pulli see?"
Sidhu thought hard. He looked at the slices in a row. "First a tiny dot," he said slowly. "Then a small circle. Then it grows bigger and bigger. Then it shrinks, and it's gone."
"Yes," said Kayal. "Pulli would never see the whole lemon at once. She would meet it one flat slice at a time."
"Poor Pulli," said Sidhu.
"Maybe not poor," said Amma. "Pulli knows her flat world very well. She knows every wall and every door in it. She just cannot see the up direction that we can."
That night, Sidhu lay on his mat and looked up at the ceiling fan going round. "Kayal," he whispered. "Is there a direction that we have never seen? Like up is for Pulli?"
Kayal thought for a long time. "I don't know," she said. "Ask Amma."
Amma sat down beside them. "Some scientists wonder about that too," she said. "They ask whether there could be more than three directions. Nobody has found one yet. It is still a question."
Sidhu smiled in the dark. "Then we are a bit like Pulli," he said.

The next morning, Sidhu took the paper and a pencil. Next to Pulli's house, he drew a park with a swing, a road and a friend for her to visit. Then he stopped. "Kayal," he said, "how will Pulli and her friend pass each other on the road? They can't climb over each other." Kayal laughed. "Make the road wider," she said.
story.epiphany: Pulli lives in a flat world with only two directions, so she can never go up, and she meets a solid lemon one flat slice at a time. We live with three directions: length, width and height. Whether there is a fourth, nobody knows yet.
ask: Why could Pulli not step over the pencil line round her house?
Sidhu looked at the coin with his eye level with the paper. What did he see, and why?
How could Pulli tell a round coin from a square card?
What would Pulli see if a lemon passed down through her flat world?
Sidhu asked if there is a direction we have never seen. What do you think? Why?

games.title: Solid and Shape: a matching card game
games.context: This is a memory card game. Each solid card is matched with a flat shape that one of the solid's faces or slices makes. To keep a pair, you must say why they match.

img.credit: PierreSelim, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

rules: Cut out the 12 cards. Mix them up and lay them face down in rows.
On your turn, turn over two cards.
If one is a solid and one is a flat shape, say how that solid could make that shape. Use its face, or a slice cut from it.
If the other players agree, keep the pair and have another turn. If not, turn both cards back over.
Many solids can make more than one shape. A birthday cap has a round end, and looks like a triangle from the side. Any match you can explain counts.
When all the cards are matched, the player with the most pairs wins.

setup.art: Twelve small cards face down in three rows on a mat.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the cards face down.

setup.art: Two cards turned up: 'Solid: a dice' and 'Flat shape: a square', with a girl pointing at a real dice.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over two. Say how the solid makes the shape.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Read the rules aloud. 3. Put a real dice, a matchbox and a tumbler on the table to look at.
flow.say: Turn over two cards. If a solid and a flat shape match, tell us how. A face counts, and a slice counts.
flow.kid: Turn over two cards. Say how the solid makes the flat shape.
flow.context: This is the start of the matching card game.

flow.do: 1. Play until all the cards are matched. 2. Ask each player to explain their match.
flow.say: Dice and square? How does a dice make a square? Ladoo and circle? Where is the circle in a ladoo?
flow.kid: Say how they match. Is it a face or a slice?

ask.q: Where is the circle in a ladoo?
good: If you cut it across, the slice is a circle.
It has no flat face, but its slices are circles.

flow.parent: A ladoo has no flat face, but every slice of it is a circle. A samosa has triangle faces. A steel tumbler has a circle at the bottom.

flow.do: 1. Count the pairs. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Which match was hardest to explain? Why?
flow.kid: Which match was hardest? Why?

check.q: In the matching card game, how can a ladoo make a circle?
options: Its flat face is a circle
A slice cut across it is a circle
It can't make any flat shape
check.why: A ladoo is a sphere, so it has no flat face. But cut it straight across, and the cut side is a circle.

games.title: Feely Bag: name the solid by touch
games.context: This is a guessing game. Solid things are hidden in a cloth bag. You feel one without looking, and say what solid shape it is and how many flat faces it has.
rules: A grown-up puts 5 solid things into a cloth bag or a pillow cover: for example, a small ball, a dice, a matchbox, a closed round tin and an orange.
On your turn, put one hand in the bag. Don't look.
Feel one thing. Say its solid shape name: sphere, cube, cuboid, cylinder or cone.
Say how many flat faces it has. Then pull it out to check.
You get 1 point for the right shape name, and 1 point for the right number of flat faces.
Write your points on the score sheet. The most points after 3 rounds wins.

setup.art: A cloth bag on a table, with a ball, a dice, a matchbox, a closed round tin and an orange beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Put 5 solids in a cloth bag.

setup.art: A boy with his hand inside the bag and his eyes looking up, feeling a dice.
setup.caption: 2. Feel one without looking. Name it.

flow.do: 1. Put 5 solids in the bag while the players are not looking. 2. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: Put your hand in. Don't look. Feel the faces and the edges. What solid is it?
flow.kid: Put your hand in the bag. Don't look. What solid is it?
flow.context: This is the start of the feely bag game.

flow.do: 1. Each player takes a turn. 2. After each guess, they pull the thing out to check. 3. Put it back and shake the bag.
flow.say: How did you know? Was it the flat faces, the edges or the curved side?
flow.kid: How did you know? Faces, edges or a curved side?

ask.q: How did you know it was a cube?
good: It had flat square faces.
It had sharp edges and corners.

flow.parent: Touch is a good way to feel faces and edges, because hands work in all three directions at once.

flow.do: 1. Add up the points. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Which solid was easiest to feel? Which was hardest?
flow.kid: Which solid was easiest to guess? Why?

check.q: In the feely bag game, you feel a thing with no flat faces and no edges at all. What solid is it?
check.why: A sphere, like a ball, is curved all over. A cube has 6 flat faces, and a cylinder has 2 flat round faces.

experiments.title: Slice and Trace: what flat shapes are hidden inside a solid?
experiments.context: In this experiment a grown-up cuts a cucumber, a carrot and a round potato straight across. You trace the flat shape of each cut side on paper. Then you find out what shape you get when you cut a corner off a potato cube.
experiments.question: When you cut a solid straight through, what flat shape do you see? Is it the same shape and size wherever you cut?
experiments.predict: If we cut the cucumber, the carrot and the round potato straight across, what shape will each cut side be? Will all the slices be the same size? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The grown-up cuts straight down every time, with the knife upright, because a slanting cut changes the shape. We trace every cut side the same way: press it on the paper and draw round it. Only the solid, and the place where we cut, change.

materials.item: a cucumber
a carrot
round potatoes, about the size of a fist
a kitchen knife and a chopping board, for the grown-up
2 sheets of paper and a pencil
a plate for the slices

experiments.safety: Only the grown-up uses the knife. The child keeps both hands on the paper while the grown-up cuts.

schedule.what: Cut the cucumber, the carrot and a round potato across, and trace each cut side. Then cut a corner off a potato cube and trace that.

experiments.record: The traced shapes, in rows: cucumber, carrot, potato and the cube corner. Under each row, write 'same size', 'smaller and smaller' or 'small, big, small'.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results, from Gowri's flat in Hyderabad
rows: nearly the same size each time
smaller and smaller towards the tip
small at the top, biggest in the middle, small at the bottom

setup.art: A cucumber, a carrot and a round potato on a chopping board, with a sheet of paper and a pencil beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Look at each solid. Guess the shape of the cut side.

setup.art: A grown-up's hands cutting a cucumber straight across with the knife upright, and a round slice falling away.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up cuts straight across.

setup.art: A child pressing a potato slice flat on paper and drawing round it with a pencil.
setup.caption: 3. Press the cut side on the paper. Draw round it.

setup.art: A rough potato cube with one corner cut off, showing a small triangle where the corner was.
setup.caption: 4. Cut a corner off a potato cube. What shape is it?

flow.do: 1. Put the cucumber, the carrot and one round potato on the board. 2. Ask the questions below. 3. Write your child's guesses at the top of the paper. Don't say who is right.
flow.say: If I cut each of these straight across, what shape will the cut side be? Will every slice be the same size? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the three vegetables. What shape will the cut side be? Will every slice be the same size? Why?

ask.q: What shape will the cut side be, and will all the slices be the same size? Why?
good: A circle, because they are round.
The same size, because it's the same vegetable.
Smaller at the ends, because the ends are thin.

flow.parent: Most children guess a circle for all three. Many guess that every slice will be the same size. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the slice and trace test. You make your guesses.

flow.do: 1. Cut the cucumber straight across in three places. 2. Cut one hand-width from each end, and one in the middle. 3. Your child presses each cut side on the paper and draws round it. 4. Write 'cucumber' under the three shapes.
flow.say: Press the cut side down on the paper and draw round it. Now the next one. Are they the same shape? Are they the same size?
flow.kid: Press the slice on the paper. Draw round it. Is the next one the same size?

ask.q: Are the three cucumber circles the same size?
good: Almost the same.
Yes, nearly.

flow.parent: A cucumber is nearly a cylinder, so the circles come out nearly the same size. Keep the cuts away from the very ends, where the cucumber gets thinner.
flow.context: In this step of the slice and trace test, you trace three slices of cucumber.

flow.do: 1. Cut the carrot straight across at three places: near the thick top, in the middle, and near the thin tip. 2. Your child traces each cut side in a new row, in the same order. 3. Write 'carrot' under the row.
flow.say: Now the carrot. Trace the thick end first, then the middle, then near the tip. What happens to the circles?
flow.kid: Trace the carrot slices, thick end first. What happens to the circles?

ask.q: What happened to the carrot circles?
good: They got smaller.
Smaller and smaller towards the tip.

flow.parent: A carrot is shaped like a long cone, so its circles get smaller towards the tip.
flow.context: In this step of the slice and trace test, you trace slices of carrot.

flow.do: 1. Cut the round potato straight across into 5 slices, from top to bottom. 2. Lay them on the plate in order. 3. Your child traces them in a new row, in the same order. 4. Then your child stacks the slices back up.
flow.say: Trace the slices in order, from the top of the potato to the bottom. Which circle is the biggest? Now stack the slices back up. What do you get?
flow.kid: Trace the potato slices in order. Which is biggest? Now stack them back up.

ask.q: Which potato slice was the biggest, and what did the stacked slices make?
good: The middle one.
The potato again.

flow.parent: The top and bottom slices are small, and the middle slice is the biggest. A potato is not a perfect ball, so the shapes may be ovals more than circles. That is fine.
flow.context: In this step of the slice and trace test, you slice a round potato and put it back together.

flow.do: 1. Cut the second potato into a rough cube by cutting off a slice from each of its 6 sides. 2. Ask your child to guess the shape if you cut off one corner. 3. Cut one corner off, about 1 centimetre in from the tip. 4. Your child traces the cut side.
flow.say: This potato is now a cube, with square faces. If I cut off one corner, what shape will the cut side be? Why?
flow.kid: This potato is now a cube. Cut off a corner. What shape will it be?

ask.q: What shape did the corner make?
good: A triangle.
A shape with three sides.

flow.parent: Most children guess a square, because the cube has square faces. The corner cut makes a triangle, because the knife cuts across three faces that meet at the corner. Cut off only the tip of the corner, or the shape gets more sides.
flow.context: In this step of the slice and trace test, you cut a corner off a potato cube.

flow.do: 1. Look at all the rows of traced shapes together. 2. Ask the questions below. 3. Then read the cards on slices.
flow.say: Look at all the shapes you traced. Were they flat or solid? Did the same vegetable always give the same size?
flow.kid: Look at your shapes. Are they flat? Did the size change?

ask.q: What changed the shape and size of the cut side?
good: Where we cut.
Which vegetable it was.
Cutting the corner made a triangle.

check.q: In the slice and trace test, where did the round potato give its biggest slice?
check.why: A round potato is widest in the middle, so the middle slice is the biggest. The slices near the top and the bottom are small.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses the traced shapes as evidence: every cut side was flat, and its size depended on where the cut was.
flow.context: This is the last step of the slice and trace test. You look at your results and say what you found.

experiments.title: Flat Eyes: can a flat creature tell a circle from a square?
experiments.context: A flat creature living on a table top would see every shape on the table from its edge. In this experiment you put your eye level with a table and look at a card circle and a card square, the way she would.
experiments.question: With your eye level with the table, can you tell a circle from a square?
experiments.predict: When your eye is level with the table, what will a card circle and a card square look like? Can you tell them apart? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The circle and the square are the same width, and cut from the same card. The child keeps their chin on the table edge every time, so the eye stays level. We turn each shape slowly all the way round, and watch the width of the line.

Did the line get wider or narrower as it turned?

materials.item: thin card from an empty sweet box or cereal box
a steel bowl or tumbler, about 8 centimetres wide, to draw round
scissors and a ruler
a table

experiments.safety: A grown-up does the cutting with scissors.

schedule.what: Cut a card circle and a card square. Look at them with your eye level with the table, and turn them.

experiments.record: Draw what each shape looked like from the edge. Write 'stays the same' or 'gets wider and narrower' under each.

setup.art: A card circle and a card square of the same width lying flat on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Lay a card circle and a card square flat on the table.

setup.art: A child with her chin resting on the edge of a table, one eye closed, looking along the table top at the shapes.
setup.caption: 2. Put your chin on the table edge. Look along the table.

setup.art: A grown-up's finger slowly turning the card square on the table, while the child watches the edge.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up turns each shape slowly. Watch the line.

flow.do: 1. Draw round the bowl on the card to make a circle. 2. Draw a square with sides the same as the circle is wide. 3. Cut out both shapes.
flow.say: Here is a circle and a square, the same width. Pulli the flat girl lives on the table. She sees them only from the edge.
flow.kid: Here is a card circle and a card square. They are the same width.
flow.parent: An 8 centimetre circle and an 8 centimetre square work well.
flow.context: This is the first step of the flat eyes test. You make the shapes.

flow.do: 1. Ask the question below. 2. Write down your child's guess.
flow.say: With your eye flat to the table, what will they look like? Will you be able to tell them apart? Why?
flow.kid: With your eye flat to the table, what will you see? Why?

ask.q: Will you be able to tell the circle from the square from the edge? Why?
good: No, they will both look like lines.
Yes, because the square has corners.

flow.context: In this step of the flat eyes test, you make your guess.

flow.do: 1. Lay both shapes flat in the middle of the table, a hand apart. 2. Your child rests their chin on the table edge and closes one eye. 3. Ask what they see.
flow.say: Chin on the table. Close one eye. What do the circle and the square look like now?
flow.kid: Put your chin on the table. Close one eye. What do you see?

ask.q: What do the shapes look like from the edge?
good: Thin lines.
Like strips.
I can't see which is which.

flow.parent: From the edge, both look like thin strips about the same width. The child cannot tell them apart from one view.
flow.context: In this step of the flat eyes test, you look at the shapes from the edge.

flow.do: 1. Slowly turn the square all the way round, while your child watches. 2. Then turn the circle the same way.
flow.say: Watch the line while I turn the square. Does it get wider? Now watch the circle. Does its line change?
flow.kid: Watch the line as the square turns. Now watch the circle.

ask.q: Which shape's line changed as it turned?
good: The square got wider and then narrower.
The circle stayed the same.

check.q: In the flat eyes test, how could a flat creature tell a circle from a square?
options: As it turns, the square's line gets wider at the corners, but the circle's line stays the same
She can never tell them apart
check.why: From the edge, both shapes look like lines. But a square is wider from corner to corner than from side to side. A circle is the same width every way. So by turning the shapes, or walking round them, a flat creature can tell them apart.

flow.parent: The square's line grows when a corner points at the eye, and shrinks again. The circle's line stays the same. A strong answer says that walking round a shape gives more clues than one look.
flow.context: This is the last step of the flat eyes test. You turn the shapes and compare.

activities.title: Flat or Solid Hunt: what has height?
activities.context: In this activity you hunt your home for things that look flat and things that are solid. Then you test a sheet of paper to see if it has any height at all.

materials.item: a notebook or a stack of about 100 sheets of paper
a ruler
a sheet of paper and a pencil

activities.record: Two lists: 'Looks flat' and 'Clearly solid'. Then write how tall the pile of paper was.

setup.art: A child holding up a chapati in one hand and a steel tumbler in the other.
setup.caption: 1. Find things that look flat and things that are solid.

setup.art: A ruler standing next to a thick notebook, showing it is about 1 centimetre tall.
setup.caption: 2. Measure the height of a pile of paper.

flow.do: 1. Give your child 3 minutes to find 4 things that look flat and 4 things that are clearly solid. 2. Write them in two lists.
flow.say: Find four things that look flat, and four things that are clearly solid. A solid has height, so it stands up off the table.
flow.kid: Find four things that look flat. Find four things that are solid.

ask.q: What did you find?
good: A chapati, a paper, a photo, a dosa.
A ball, a tumbler, a box, a pillow.

flow.parent: Good flat-looking finds: a sheet of paper, a photo, a chapati, a playing card, a kolam or rangoli. Good solid finds: a ball, a tumbler, a box, a ladoo.
flow.context: This is the first step of the flat or solid hunt.

flow.do: 1. Pick up one sheet of paper and ask the question below. 2. Then stand a ruler next to a notebook of about 100 sheets. 3. Read the height together.
flow.say: Is this sheet of paper truly flat, with no height at all? Let's look at a pile of 100 sheets. How tall is the pile?
flow.kid: Is one sheet of paper truly flat? Look at a pile of 100 sheets.

ask.q: What does the pile tell you about one sheet?
good: Each sheet has a tiny height.
Paper is a very thin solid.

check.q: A pile of 100 sheets of paper is about 1 centimetre tall. What does that tell you?
options: Paper has no height at all
Each sheet has a tiny height, so paper is a very thin solid
Only the top sheet has height
check.why: If the sheets had no height, 100 of them would make no pile at all. The pile is 1 centimetre tall, so each sheet has a tiny height.

flow.parent: Most notebooks of 100 sheets are about 1 centimetre thick, without the cover. A pile of 200 pages printed on both sides is the same as 100 sheets.
flow.context: This is the last step of the flat or solid hunt. You find out whether paper has height.

activities.title: Open a Box: from solid to flat and back
activities.context: In this activity you open an empty box out flat, to see the flat net it was made from. Then you fold it back into a solid box.

materials.item: an empty small box, such as a toothpaste box or a sweet box
a pencil and a sheet of paper
a little sticky tape

activities.record: Trace round the opened-out box on paper. Number its faces. Write how many faces it has.

setup.art: A grown-up and a child gently pulling apart the glued flap of a toothpaste box.
setup.caption: 1. Open the glued flaps gently.

setup.art: The same box lying open and flat on the floor, as a long cross of rectangles, with faces numbered 1 to 6.
setup.caption: 2. Lay it flat and count its faces.

setup.art: A child folding the flat net back up into a box.
setup.caption: 3. Fold it back into a box.

flow.do: 1. Hold up the closed box. 2. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: This box is a solid. How many faces does it have? What do you think it will look like if we open it out flat?
flow.kid: How many faces does the box have? What will it look like opened flat?

ask.q: How many faces does the box have?
good: Top, bottom, front, back and two sides.

flow.context: This is the first step of Open a Box.

flow.do: 1. Gently pull apart the glued flap and open the end flaps. 2. Lay the box out flat. 3. Your child traces round it on paper. 4. Number each face.
flow.say: Let's open it out without tearing it. Now it's flat. Count the faces. Are they all still here?
flow.kid: Open the box gently. Lay it flat. Count the faces.
flow.parent: Pull the glued flap slowly, so the card does not tear. The flat shape is called a net. Small flaps that tucked in are not faces.
flow.context: In this step of Open a Box, you open the box out flat.

flow.do: 1. Your child folds the net back into a box along the old folds. 2. Tape the glued flap. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Fold it back up along the old lines. Is it the same box again? Where did the height come from?
flow.kid: Fold it back up. Is it a box again?

ask.q: The net was flat. How did it become a solid?
good: We folded it up.
Folding gave it height.

check.q: In Open a Box, what is the flat shape you get when you open a box out?
check.why: A net is a flat shape that folds up into a solid. A slice is what you cut off a solid, and a face is one flat side of it.

flow.parent: Folding is how a flat sheet becomes a solid. Lifting each face up off the floor gives the box its height.
flow.context: This is the last step of Open a Box. You fold the net back into a solid.

activities.title: Stack It Up: from flat to solid
activities.context: In this activity you stack thin, flat-looking things on top of each other, and watch them become a solid with real height.

materials.item: about 20 coins, or round biscuits
about 20 playing cards or old postcards
a ruler

activities.record: Draw your two towers. Write how many pieces were in each, and how tall each tower was.

setup.art: A child stacking coins one on top of another into a short tower.
setup.caption: 1. Stack coins one on top of another.

setup.art: Two towers on a table, one of coins and one of cards, with a ruler beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Measure each tower.

flow.do: 1. Your child stacks 20 coins into a tower. 2. Then stacks 20 cards into a second pile. 3. Ask what shape each tower is.
flow.say: Each coin is a short, flat-looking circle. Stack twenty. What shape have you made? Now stack the cards. What shape is that?
flow.kid: Stack twenty coins. What shape is the tower? Now stack the cards.

ask.q: What solid shapes did the towers make?
good: The coins made a cylinder.
The cards made a cuboid, like a box.

flow.context: This is the first step of Stack It Up.

flow.do: 1. Measure each tower with the ruler. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: How tall is each tower? Each piece added a little height. What happens if we keep on stacking?
flow.kid: How tall is each tower? What if you keep stacking?

ask.q: Where did the tower's height come from?
good: From every coin.
Each piece has a tiny height, and they add up.

flow.parent: 20 coins make a tower a few centimetres tall. 20 playing cards make a pile less than 1 centimetre tall. The exact number does not matter. What matters is that small heights add up.
flow.context: This is the last step of Stack It Up. You measure the towers.

projects.title: A Town for Pulli: design a flat world
projects.context: In this project you design a town for Pulli, the flat girl who lives on paper. She can only move forward, back, left and right. On day 2 you solve the problems that a flat world brings.

materials.item: a big sheet of paper, or newspaper with a blank side
a pencil, an eraser and crayons
a coin or a button to be Pulli

schedule.what: Draw Pulli's town from above: houses with doors, a road, a school and a shop.
Slide the coin Pulli round the town. Solve the problems: doors, passing a friend, and crossing a road.

projects.record: The finished town map, with notes on how Pulli gets in and out of her house and how she passes a friend.

setup.art: A town drawn on paper from above: square houses with gaps for doors, a road and a school.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a flat town from above.

setup.art: A coin being slid along a drawn road towards a house door, with a second coin coming the other way.
setup.caption: 2. Slide the coin Pulli round the town.

flow.do: 1. Remind your child that Pulli cannot go over any line. 2. Your child draws a town from above, with at least 3 houses, a road, a school and a shop. 3. Every building needs a door.
flow.say: Pulli can't step over a line. So every house needs a gap for a door. Draw her a town she can move round.
flow.kid: Draw a town for Pulli. Every house needs a door gap.

ask.q: How does Pulli get into her house?
good: Through the gap in the wall.
She can't climb over, so she needs a door.

flow.context: This is day 1 of A Town for Pulli.

flow.do: 1. Your child slides a coin along the roads as Pulli. 2. Put a second coin on the same road, coming the other way. 3. Ask the questions below. 4. Your child changes the drawing to fix each problem.
flow.say: Pulli meets her friend on a narrow road. Neither can go over the other. What can they do? If Pulli's door is open, is her house still closed in?
flow.kid: Pulli meets a friend on the road. How can they pass?

ask.q: How can Pulli pass her friend on a narrow road?
good: Make the road wider.
Add a side road for one to wait in.

ask.q: What happens to Pulli's house when her door is open?
good: Anyone can come in.
The wall has a gap, so it isn't closed.

check.q: In A Town for Pulli, why can't Pulli step over a wall?
options: She has no up direction, so she can't go over a line
check.why: Stepping over means going up and then down. Pulli's world has only forward, back, left and right, so any line is a wall for her.

flow.parent: Children often find new problems: a door that opens swings into the room and blocks it, and a drawn road splits the town in two for Pulli. Praise every problem they find. Each one shows what the up direction does for us.
flow.context: This is day 2 of A Town for Pulli.

challenges.title: Hold It Up with One Flat Sheet
challenges.context: This is a building challenge. A flat sheet of paper flops over. Can you fold or roll it into a solid that holds a steel plate up off the table?
challenges.problem: Use one sheet of paper to hold a steel plate at least 5 centimetres above the table.
constraints: Use only one sheet of paper, about the size of a notebook page.
You may use 2 short pieces of sticky tape.
The plate must stay up for 10 seconds.
general: Roll the paper into a wide, short tube, with the long side going round, and stand it on its end.
Fold the paper into a triangle tube and stand it up.
creative: Cut the sheet into three strips and roll three short tubes, to make three legs.
Fold the paper back and forth like a fan, and stand it in a ring.
challenges.your_turn: Find your own way to make the flat sheet hold up the plate. Then try to hold up a book.

setup.art: A flat sheet of paper flopping over on a table, with a steel plate beside it.
setup.caption: 1. A flat sheet can't hold up the plate.

setup.art: A sheet rolled into a tall tube, standing up with a steel plate balanced on top.
setup.caption: 2. Roll or fold the sheet into a solid. Try again.

flow.do: 1. Stand the flat sheet up on its edge and let it flop. 2. Explain the challenge.
flow.say: This flat sheet flops over. Can you make it hold up a steel plate, using only this one sheet and two pieces of tape?
flow.kid: Can one flat sheet hold up a steel plate?

ask.q: What could you do to the sheet?
good: Roll it.
Fold it.
Make it into a tube.

flow.do: 1. Your child tries ways to fold or roll the sheet. 2. Test each one with the plate. 3. Measure the height with the ruler.
flow.say: Try it. Does it hold the plate? How high is the plate now?
flow.kid: Try it. Does it hold the plate? How high?
flow.parent: A tube rolled from a notebook page, about 6 centimetres wide, usually holds a small steel plate easily. If the plate tips, tape the tube to keep it from unrolling.

flow.do: 1. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: The flat sheet flopped. What changed when you rolled it?
flow.kid: What changed when you rolled the sheet?

check.q: Why could the rolled sheet hold the plate when the flat sheet could not?
options: Rolling made a solid tube with height and width, which stands up
check.why: A flat sheet is very thin, so it bends and falls. Rolled into a tube, the paper spreads round in a circle and goes up. The tube is a solid shape, and it stands firm.

quiz.p: Which of these is a flat (2D) shape?
quiz.why: A circle drawn on paper has length and width but no height. A ladoo and a tumbler have height, so they are solids.

quiz.p: A solid shape has three dimensions. What are they?
quiz.why: A solid can be measured three ways: how long, how wide and how tall.
A dice has 6 square faces, so it is a cube. A sphere is round like a ball, and a cone has a point.

quiz.p: How many faces does a matchbox have?
quiz.why: A matchbox has a top, a bottom, a front, a back and two ends. That is 6 faces.

quiz.p: In the slice and trace test, what happened to the carrot slices from the thick end to the tip?
quiz.why: A carrot gets thinner towards the tip, like a long cone, so its circles get smaller.
quiz.context: This question is about the slice and trace test. A grown-up cut a cucumber, a carrot and a round potato, and you traced each cut side.

quiz.p: What shape did a grown-up get by cutting a corner off a potato cube?
quiz.why: The cut crosses the three faces that meet at the corner, so the new face has three sides: a triangle. Choosing the square means thinking a cube can only give squares.

opts: A flat shape that folds up into a solid
quiz.why: When you opened out a box, you got its net: a flat shape that folds back into the box.

quiz.p: Pulli is a flat girl who lives on paper. Which of these can she never do?
quiz.why: Pulli's world has forward, back, left and right, but no up. So she can never jump up or step over a line.

quiz.p: A ball passes slowly down through Pulli's flat world. What does she see?
opts: A circle that grows and then shrinks
quiz.why: Pulli meets the ball one flat slice at a time. The slices grow to the biggest in the middle, then shrink, like the round potato slices.

quiz.p: Is a sheet of paper truly flat, with no height at all?
opts: No, it is a very thin solid
quiz.why: A pile of 100 sheets is about 1 centimetre tall, so each sheet has a tiny height.

quiz.p: Is there a fourth direction, beyond length, width and height?
opts: No, scientists have proved there is none
quiz.why: Some scientists think there might be more directions, too small or too hidden to notice. Nobody has found one. It is still an open question.

items.p: Draw a line from each word to what it means.
pairs: has length and width, but no height
a flat side of a solid
a flat shape that folds up into a solid
items.why: These are the four words the child needs most in this unit. A solid has one more direction than a flat shape: height.

items.p: Sort these into 'flat shape' and 'solid shape'.
items: a circle drawn on a slate
items.why: Drawn shapes have only length and width. The ladoo, the tumbler and the matchbox have height too, so they are solids.

items.p: In the slice and trace test, what shape was the cut side of a cucumber slice?
items.why: A cucumber is nearly a cylinder, so a straight cut across it gives a circle. Choosing the square may mean thinking of the whole vegetable, not the cut side.
items.context: This question is about the slice and trace test. A grown-up cut a cucumber, a carrot and a round potato, and you traced each cut side.

items.p: Draw the three slices of carrot you traced: from the thick end, the middle and near the tip.
items.a: Three circles that get smaller and smaller.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the circle from the thick end biggest, and the one near the tip smallest, because a carrot gets thinner towards the tip.
items.context: This question is about the slice and trace test. A grown-up cut a cucumber, a carrot and a round potato, and you traced each cut side.

items.p: A sheet of paper has no height at all.
items.why: False. A pile of 100 sheets is about 1 centimetre tall, so each sheet has a tiny height. Paper is a very thin solid.

items.p: Meenakshi opened a sweet box out flat. She counted the faces of the net. How many faces does a box have?
items.why: A box has a top, a bottom, a front, a back and two sides. That is 6 faces. Opening it out flat does not take any faces away.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: what can you do that Pulli the flat girl can never do?
items.a: For example: I can jump up, or step over a line.
items.why: A strong answer names something that needs the up direction, such as jumping, climbing or stepping over a wall.

items.p: Farhana and Divya are looking at a dosa on a plate.

views.says: A dosa is a flat shape, like a circle drawn on paper.
A dosa is a solid. It is just very thin.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other girl has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Divya, because you can lift a dosa and it has a top and a bottom, so it has a little height. It also says Farhana is right that a dosa is round and very thin, so it looks almost flat.
items.why: Both have part of it. The outline of a dosa is a circle, and the dosa is thin. But a dosa has a top and a bottom, so it has height and is a solid. The paper pile test is the evidence that even very thin things have height.

items.p: Look at the drawing of a matchbox. Write 'length', 'width' and 'height' on the three arrows.
labels: the long arrow along the bottom
the short arrow across the bottom
a: the long arrow along the bottom: length
the short arrow across the bottom: width
items.why: Length is the long way, width is from side to side, and height is up. A solid like a matchbox has all three.
items.art: A matchbox with three arrows: a long one along the bottom edge, a short one across the bottom, and one going up a corner.

items.p: Three of these are solid shapes. Which one is a flat shape?
items.why: A square drawn on paper has length and width but no height. The ball, the dice and the tumbler all have height, so they are solids.

items.p: In the slice and trace test, the round potato was cut into 5 slices from top to bottom. Which slice was the biggest?
items.why: A round potato is widest in the middle, so the middle slice is the biggest circle. Choosing the top or bottom may mean thinking every slice of a solid is the same size.
items.context: This question is about the slice and trace test. A grown-up cut a cucumber, a carrot and a round potato, and you traced each cut side.

items.p: Put the slices of a round potato in order, from the top of the potato to the bottom.
items.why: A round potato is narrow at the top, widest in the middle, and narrow again at the bottom. So the slices grow, then shrink.

items.p: Draw what Pulli the flat girl would see as a ball passed slowly down through her flat world. Draw 4 boxes, one after another.
items.a: A dot, a small circle, a big circle, a small circle (or a dot).
items.why: Pulli meets the ball one flat slice at a time. The slices start small, grow to the biggest in the middle of the ball, and shrink again, like the potato slices.

items.p: A flat creature can move forward and back, and left and right. She can never move ________.
items.why: A flat world has only two directions. Up and down is the third direction, which solids have and flat shapes do not.

items.p: In the flat eyes test, a card circle and a card square both looked like lines from the edge. How could you tell them apart?
items.a: Turn them, or walk round them. The square's line got wider at the corners, but the circle's line stayed the same.
items.why: A strong answer uses what was seen when the shapes turned: a square is wider from corner to corner, but a circle is the same width every way.

items.p: Lakshmi and Arjun are talking about the potato cube from the slice and trace test.

views.says: A cube has square faces, so every cut you make will be a square.
When we cut off a corner, we got a triangle. So a cube can give other shapes too.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give your reason. Then say why the other idea makes sense at first.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Arjun, because the corner cut gave a triangle. It also says Lakshmi's idea makes sense, because a cube's faces are squares, and a cut straight across the middle, side to side, does give a square.
items.why: The shape of a slice depends on where you cut. A cut parallel to a face gives a square. A cut across a corner gives a triangle. The traced triangle is the evidence.

items.p: Look at the drawing of a steel tumbler. Write 'flat face', 'curved side' and 'edge' in the right places.
labels: the line where the bottom meets the side
a: the line where the bottom meets the side: edge
items.why: A tumbler has a flat round face at the bottom and a curved side. An edge is where two parts of a solid meet.
items.art: A steel tumbler drawn from the side, with arrows to the bottom, the side and the bottom rim.

items.p: Revathi stacked 10 playing cards, then 10 more, then 10 more. How many cards are in her pile?
items.why: 10 and 10 and 10 make 30. Each card adds a tiny height, so 30 cards make a taller solid pile than 10.

items.p: A ball has no flat faces at all.
items.why: True. A ball is a sphere, curved all over. Its slices are flat circles, but its outside has no flat face.

items.p: Sort these solids into 'can roll' and 'can't roll'.
items: a steel tumbler on its side
items.why: Solids with a curved side, like a ball, a lemon or a tumbler on its side, can roll. Solids with only flat faces, like a dice or a matchbox, slide or tumble instead.

items.p: Pulli lives in a flat world. Why is a circle drawn round her a wall she can never get past?
items.a: Getting past a line means stepping over it, and stepping over needs the up direction. Pulli's world has no up.
items.why: A strong answer says that going over something needs a third direction, height, which a flat world does not have.

items.p: Tanvi cut a carrot straight across, but she slanted the knife. What shape did the cut side make?
opts: A stretched circle, called an oval
items.why: A slanting cut goes across the carrot at an angle, so the circle is stretched into an oval. The shape of a slice depends on how you cut, not only on the solid.

items.p: Draw a net that would fold up into a dice. Use 6 squares joined at their sides.
items.a: Six squares joined edge to edge, for example in a cross shape.
items.why: A strong drawing has 6 squares, all joined along whole sides, arranged so they can fold up without two squares landing on the same face. A cross shape works. Six squares in one long row does not.

items.p: Nithya and her grandfather are talking about the ground under their feet.

views.says: The ground looks flat, so the Earth must be flat.
The Earth is a huge ball. A small piece of a huge ball looks flat.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one piece of evidence. Then say why the other idea makes sense at first.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Nithya, and gives evidence such as the round shadow of the Earth on the Moon, or photos from space. It also says the grandfather's idea makes sense, because the ground near us really does look flat.
items.why: The Earth is a solid ball, but it is so big that the piece we stand on looks almost flat. Aristotle saw that the Earth's shadow on the Moon is always round, and only a ball does that.

items.p: Your potato slices stacked back into a potato. Use this to explain how a solid is different from a flat shape.
items.a: A solid is like flat slices piled up. The pile gives it height, which a flat shape does not have.
items.why: A strong answer uses the stacked slices as evidence: each slice is a flat shape, and piling them up in the up direction makes a solid.

items.p: Three of these have flat faces. Which one has no flat face at all?
items.why: A lemon is curved all over, like a sphere. The dice, the matchbox and the samosa all have flat faces.

items.p: Mou traced 3 cucumber slices, 3 carrot slices and 5 potato slices. How many shapes did she trace?
items.why: 3 and 3 make 6, and 6 and 5 make 11. Every one of the 11 shapes is flat, though they came from solids.

items.p: Look at the drawing of a potato cube with its corner cut off. Label the square face and the triangle.
labels: the big face on the front
the small new face where the corner was
a: the big face on the front: square
the small new face where the corner was: triangle
items.why: The cube's own faces are squares. Cutting off a corner makes a new flat face, and it is a triangle, because the cut crosses three faces.
items.art: A rough potato cube with one corner sliced off, showing a small triangle face.

items.p: A flat creature looks at a card square lying in her flat world. What does she see?
items.why: She can only look along her flat world, so she sees the square from its edge, as a line. In the flat eyes test, the card shapes looked like lines when your eye was level with the table.

items.p: Some scientists ask whether there could be more than three directions. Why would it be hard for us to find out?
items.a: We have never seen a fourth direction, just as Pulli has never seen up. We might only see slices of things that go into it.
items.why: A strong answer compares us with Pulli: a flat creature meets a ball only as circles, so we might meet things in a fourth direction only as solids. Nobody knows yet whether a fourth direction exists.

applications: Box makers print a flat net on card, then fold it into a box. Every sweet box and medicine box starts flat.
Doctors use CT scanners to take many flat slice pictures of a body. A computer stacks the slices to show the solid shape inside.
Architects draw flat plans of each floor of a building. Builders use them to make the solid building.
Artists draw solid things on flat paper, making far parts smaller, so the drawing looks deep.
Maryam Mirzakhani, a mathematician from Iran, studied the shapes of curved surfaces. In 2014 she became the first woman to win the Fields Medal, the top prize in mathematics.
Alicia Boole Stott never went to university. She taught herself to picture shapes with four directions, and built card models of their solid slices.

open_questions.q: Are there more than three directions in space?
open_questions.why_open: Some physicists think there could be extra directions, curled up too small to notice. Nobody has found any in an experiment. Many scientists think there are just three.

open_questions.q: Can anything real be truly flat, with no height at all?
open_questions.why_open: Even graphene, one of the thinnest materials made, is one atom thick. People still argue about whether anything real is truly 2D, or whether flat shapes are only ideas.

open_questions.q: What would it be like to live in a flat world?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody has met a flat creature. Writers and scientists imagine it to understand our own three directions better. How a flat body could eat, see or build is still a puzzle people enjoy.

maths.problem: In the slice and trace test, Sahana traced 5 potato slices. Their widths, from top to bottom, were 2, 5, 6, 5 and 2 centimetres. Which slice was widest? What pattern do you see?
maths.answer: The middle slice, at 6 centimetres. The widths grow, then shrink in the same way, so the potato is about the same at the top and the bottom.
maths.explain: 6 is the biggest number, and it is in the middle. 2 and 5 come before it, and 5 and 2 after it, like a mirror.
maths.context: This question is about the slice and trace test. A grown-up cut a cucumber, a carrot and a round potato, and you traced each cut side.
maths.why_maths: A pattern in the slice sizes tells you the shape of the whole solid, without looking at it.

maths.problem: Ishita opened out a cube-shaped box. Each face is a square. How many squares are in its net?
maths.explain: A cube has 6 faces, and every face of a cube is a square. Opening it out keeps all 6.
maths.context: This question is about Open a Box. You opened a box out flat and counted its faces.
maths.why_maths: Counting faces lets you check that a net has everything it needs to fold into the solid.

maths.problem: Gowri stacked coins into a tower. 10 coins made a tower 2 centimetres tall. How tall would 20 coins be, if every coin is the same?
maths.explain: 20 coins is two lots of 10. Each lot of 10 is 2 centimetres. 2 and 2 make 4.
maths.context: This question is about Stack It Up. You stacked coins into a tower and measured it.
maths.why_maths: Adding up the heights shows how many thin, flat-looking pieces it takes to build a solid of a certain height.

maths.problem: In the feely bag game, Thenmozhi felt 5 things. 2 had no flat faces, and the rest had flat faces. How many had flat faces?
maths.context: This question is about the feely bag game. You felt solids in a bag and counted their flat faces.
maths.why_maths: Sorting solids by their faces is how we find which ones roll and which ones stack.

maths.problem: Mou drew shapes for Pulli's town: 4 squares for houses, 1 rectangle for a school and 3 triangles for roofs. How many flat shapes did she draw? Which kind did she draw most of?
maths.explain: 4 and 1 and 3 make 8. 4 is the biggest of 4, 1 and 3, so squares are the most.
maths.context: This question is about A Town for Pulli. You drew a flat town for a flat girl.
maths.why_maths: Counting the shapes in a drawing helps you plan a flat world before you draw it.

roots.context: We have hunted for flat and solid things, sliced vegetables, looked along a table like a flat creature, and opened a box out flat. Now we ask what flat and solid tell us about the world, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: Every cut through your round potato showed a flat circle, small at the top and biggest in the middle. Stacked back up, the slices made the potato again. So a solid is flat slices piled up in a third direction, height. A flat creature could meet the potato only one slice at a time.
deep_truth.habit: We think of a solid as one lump, and of flat shapes as a different kind of thing. The slices show that a solid can be cut into flat shapes and built back from them. The difference is one extra direction.
deep_truth.evidence: In the slice and trace test, the round potato gave circles that grew and then shrank, and the stacked slices made the whole potato again.

three.who_am_i: You are a solid. You have length, width and height, and you can move in all three directions: forward and back, left and right, up and down.
three.what_is_life: Living beings use all three directions. A plant spreads their leaves flat and wide to catch light, and sends roots down into the soil. A crow flies up, down and across.
three.what_is_this_world: The world we know has three directions. A flat creature would meet our solid world one slice at a time. Nobody knows yet whether there is a fourth direction that we meet only in slices too.

roots.thread: A flat creature meets a solid one slice at a time, and we meet the world through our own three directions. Everything is conscious, and every being meets the world through their own body: an ant walking on the floor, a plant spreading leaves, and you. Many scientists disagree, and say only beings with brains are aware.

teachings.source: Plato, the Republic, Book 7: the story of the cave
teachings.teaching: Plato told of prisoners chained in a cave, facing a wall. All their lives they see only flat shadows of things moving behind them. They think the shadows are the real things.
teachings.link: Pulli sees only lines and slices of our solid world, and takes them for everything there is. Plato asked whether we too might see only part of what is real.

teachings.source: Jain teaching of anekantavada, many-sidedness, and the story of the blind men and the elephant (also told in the Buddhist Udana, 6.4)
teachings.teaching: Each blind man touches one part of an elephant: a leg, an ear, the trunk. Each says the elephant is like a pillar, a fan or a snake. Each is partly right, and none knows the whole.
teachings.link: In the slice and trace test, each slice showed one true flat shape of the potato, but no single slice showed the whole potato. To know the solid, you need all the slices together.

science.text: Every real thing we know has length, width and height. Even a sheet of paper or a sheet of graphene, one atom thick, has a tiny height.
Cutting a solid gives flat slices, and stacking the slices builds the solid again. CT scanners in hospitals use this to show the inside of a body.
Some physicists think there may be more than three directions in space, too small for us to notice. Nobody has found any.

other_view.view: Many say there are just three directions of space, and that asking about a fourth is only a game for the mind. Many also say that potatoes, paper and made-up flat creatures have no awareness at all, and that only animals with brains are aware.

practice.title: Feel your three directions
practice.say: Stand up and breathe in slowly. Stretch both arms forward and back. Now stretch them out to the left and the right. Now reach up high, and then down to your toes. Those are your three directions. Now press your palms flat together, and imagine being as flat as Pulli. Breathe out slowly.
practice.kid: Stand up. Breathe slowly. Reach forward and back. Reach left and right. Reach up, then down. Press your hands flat together. Imagine being flat.

playtest: Thought through as a parent and child in a flat. The slice and trace test needs only a cucumber, a carrot and two potatoes, found in most Indian kitchens, and the vegetables can be cooked afterwards. A grown-up does all the cutting. Fist-sized potatoes give 5 slices about 1 centimetre thick, which a 7-year-old can trace easily. Potatoes are rarely perfect balls, so the slices are often ovals, but the small, big, small pattern is always clear. The corner cut gives a clear triangle if only the tip of the corner is cut off. In the flat eyes test, 8 centimetre card shapes on a dining table work well. The square's line grows by nearly half as a corner turns towards the eye, which children can see. Toothpaste and sweet boxes open out without tearing if the glued flap is pulled slowly.

how_we_found_out.story: The ground around us looks flat. So for a long time, many people in many lands thought the Earth was flat, like a huge plate. Thinkers in ancient Greece and in India found clues that it is really a solid ball. About 2,350 years ago, the Greek thinker Aristotle watched eclipses of the Moon. In an eclipse, the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. Aristotle saw that the edge of the shadow is always curved. A flat plate would sometimes make a thin, straight shadow, but a ball makes a round shadow from every side. He also noticed that when people travel north or south, they see different stars. That happens only if the ground curves. In 499 CE, the Indian astronomer Aryabhata wrote in his book, the Aryabhatiya, that the Earth is a round ball that spins. Today, photos taken from space show the round Earth. The Earth looks flat to us because it is so big. A small piece of a huge ball is almost flat.
how_we_found_out.who: Aristotle, a thinker in ancient Greece. Aryabhata, an astronomer in India.
how_we_found_out.when: Aristotle wrote about the round shadow about 2,350 years ago. Aryabhata wrote the Aryabhatiya in 499 CE.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the Earth is flat, like a plate. The round shadow of the Earth on the Moon, and the different stars seen by travellers, showed that the Earth is a ball.
